cues: At Hindu weddings, fruit-bearing plants flank entrances, serving as auspicious decorations associated with prosperity.
Commercial growers sleeve developing bunches in perforated covers, protecting tender fruit from insects and surface blemishes.
Farmers remove the dangling male flower after fruit sets, directing growth toward more uniform clusters.
After harvest, chopped water-rich stalks are spread between rows as mulch, conserving soil moisture during dry spells.
In some tropical communities, rejected ripe fruit is mixed into animal feed, reducing waste while supplementing livestock rations.
Growers prune black-streaked leaves to limit fungal disease, protecting the canopy that nourishes developing bunches.
